title: Former FIFA Council member Johansen calls for Infantino's resignation
dek: Isha Johansen, former Sierra Leone Football Association president and ex-FIFA Council member, has publicly called for FIFA president Gianni Infantino's resignation, citing ethical breaches in his handling of the FIFA Forward Enterprise proposal. Johansen, who served on the FIFA Council from 2021, becomes the first prominent African football figure to break with continental backing for Infantino ahead of his 2027 re-election bid.
author: The GoCheckMySports Desk
key_fact: Johansen invoked Infantino's own 2021 advice to her to step down, now turning that counsel back on him and framing the FIFA Forward Enterprise as having crossed an ethical line that may have caused irreparable damage to his leadership credibility.
bottom_line: Johansen's statement represents the first major crack in African football's support for Infantino ahead of 2027 re-election. Watch whether other African officials follow her public lead, and whether Infantino or CAF leadership directly respond to her call. The outcome of any formal challenge to his re-election will depend partly on whether Johansen's ethical framing gains institutional traction beyond her voice.
body: Isha Johansen, former Sierra Leone Football Association president and ex-FIFA Council member, has publicly called on FIFA president Gianni Infantino to step down, becoming the first prominent African football leader to break ranks with continental support for his leadership. Johansen was elected to the FIFA Council in March 2021 and led the Sierra Leone Football Association from 2013 until 2021.

Johansen's demand for Infantino's resignation centers on his role in the FIFA Forward Enterprise proposal, which would have created a commercial subsidiary valued at approximately $20 billion and consolidated major FIFA revenue-generating operations, including broadcasting, sponsorship and ticketing, into the new entity with up to 20% available to outside investors. FIFA told its 211 member associations they could receive as much as $40 million each during the 2027-30 cycle if the plan went ahead.

Johansen stated, according to ESPN's reporting, that Infantino's actions with the FIFA Forward Enterprise "crossed an ethical line" and led to "a breach of trust" in his leadership "that may now be beyond repair." She emphasized that her criticism focuses on "the act, the deed, the ethics behind the proposal. How it was presented, how it was unethical. The deed, not the man himself."

The weight of Johansen's challenge lies partly in its symmetry: she recalled that Infantino personally advised her to step down during a visit to Sierra Leone around 2021, with CAF president Patrice Motsepe also present, citing that it was "a no win situation" and "for the good of football." Johansen stepped down from the SLFA presidential election in 2021, three months after her FIFA Council election, publicly citing the demands of her international responsibilities. Now she frames Infantino's resignation using his own rationale.

The FIFA Forward Enterprise proposal drew fierce opposition, particularly from UEFA, Concacaf and the Asian Football Confederation, over both its substance and the process by which it was presented. Infantino, who became FIFA president in 2016, withdrew the proposal and apologized following the opposition. Despite this reversal, Johansen maintains that the breach of governance trust cannot be repaired simply through withdrawal of the plan.

Johansen's intervention breaks a unified African stance: CAF's executive committee unanimously reaffirmed its support for Infantino and his re-election in 2027, and CAF president Patrice Motsepe publicly defended Infantino, describing the FIFA president as a loyal friend to Africa. However, Musa Bility, former Liberia Football Association president and former CAF executive committee member, has also called on CAF to reconsider its endorsement, warning that "Africa must not become the firewall protecting one man from accountability."

Johansen said Infantino is "certainly not going to go unopposed now" in the re-election, contrasting his previous status as "a shoo-in." She noted that opposition to Infantino "has hardened elsewhere" but "the response from Africa has been markedly different," indicating that her public call may signal shifting sentiment within a region that has provided his most reliable backing. Johansen detailed her governance experiences in her book "The Uncommon Enemy," which covers ethics and governance issues in football.
